govdocs-archive_org-nsia-AssassinationIn:
Robert Blair Kaiser wrote for Rolling Stone in April 1975, at a moment when Watergate had taught Americans to doubt official stories. His article of April 24 argued plainly that Congress should reopen the investigation of the Kennedy assassination.

Kaiser marshals the doubts that had accumulated since the Warren Report, and he includes remarks from a member of the Warren Commission itself. Within a few years Congress did reopen the case, creating the House Select Committee on Assassinations. The article is seventies press criticism with a result: part of the public push that forced the second investigation.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBIFainJohnWSA_:
Book V of the Church Committee's final report grades the intelligence agencies on one hard test: the investigation of President Kennedy's assassination. The Senate committee studied how the agencies had performed, with the FBI's handling of Lee Harvey Oswald at the center. It reaches back to agent John W. Fain's 1962 interview of Oswald.

Fain questioned Oswald long before Dallas, and what the Bureau did with that interview became a test of its competence. The report weighs missed chances and weak follow-up across the agencies. It remains a core official source on why the Oswald file failed to prevent the assassination.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-HeitmanWallaceS:
A Secret Service memorandum by Agent Patterson, dated November 25, 1965, reports information obtained at the Dallas office. Among it are a wife's statements about FBI contact with her husband before the assassination. She also spoke of a rifle seen at her home.

Statements like hers fed the long argument over how much the Bureau knew before Dallas. A wife's memory of agents at the door, and of a rifle in the house, carried obvious weight. The memo preserves her account as the Secret Service recorded it two years after the shooting.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KunkelRobertSA_:
The Washington Post reported that L. Patrick Gray III, the acting director of the FBI, had censured Robert Kunkel. Kunkel headed the bureau's Washington field office, one of its most sensitive posts. Gray put him on probation and transferred him to St. Louis.

A censure from the director was a serious formal punishment inside the bureau. The story belongs to the post-Hoover years, when Gray was trying to control an agency long run as one man's domain. It also shows how quickly a senior official could fall: from running the capital's field office to probation and a transfer in a single decision.

Marm Lisa is a story by Kate Douglas Wiggin, in a sixth edition of 1905. A line from Goethe's Faust opens it: the eternal-womanly leads us on. Chapter one is set in Eden Place, by Mistress Mary's garden. A strange child, Lisa, is transplanted into that garden's care.

nasa-tm-19640017346-variations-in-the-ec:
T. L. Felsentreger and J. P. Murphy of Goddard wrote this note in June 1964. Both worked in Goddard's data systems and theory offices. Their subject is the changing oval shape of one satellite's orbit. The satellite is 1962 Beta Alpha, also named Alouette in the text.

The study covers April 27, 1963 to March 8, 1964. It found a slow, long-period shift in the orbit's shape. Eccentricity is the measure of how stretched an orbit is. Even small drifts change a satellite's height pattern over months. Tracking such drift helped keep Alouette's ionosphere data tied to the right places above Earth.
nasa-tm-19690023925-laser-tracking-and-c:
H. N. Plotkin of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this October 1968 preprint, numbered X-524-69-103, on laser tracking and communication with satellites. Pulsed lasers had already tracked satellites for several years when he wrote. Four American satellites carried passive reflectors made for the purpose, and ruby lasers ranged them to about one meter of precision.

Those ranges sharpen satellite orbits, station locations, and maps of Earth's gravity field. Plotkin looks next at continuous argon and carbon dioxide laser experiments with satellites. They point toward optical communication in space, he argues. Work still needed includes handling air effects on the beam and better lasers themselves. Finer tracking could one day measure lunar motion, continental drift, and Earth's wobble.
